introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL TWO questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first 2 will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cu = 64.0, Cl = 35.5, K = 39.0, N = 14.0, S = 32.0; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; $0^\circ$C = 273 K.
enonce_intro_markdown:
Salts can be prepared in the laboratory by the following methods.

a) Neutralisation

b) Action of an acid on an insoluble base

c) Double decomposition

Using a suitable example in each case, describe how a pure dry sample of each salt can be prepared. *[7, 7, 6 marks]*
incertitudes: Section A : l'en-tête dit « ANSWER ALL 5 questions. You will be graded for the best 4 answers ». La règle structurée « 4 sur 5 » traduit la notation sur les 4 meilleures réponses ; l'élève doit tout de même traiter les 5 (le texte exact figure dans l'introduction).

questions.enonce_markdown: Neutralisation: using a suitable example, describe how a pure dry sample of the salt can be prepared. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Example: sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide (an alkali) and dilute hydrochloric acid.**

$\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

1. Use a pipette to transfer $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of sodium hydroxide solution into a clean conical flask and add 2 or 3 drops of an indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein, pink).
2. Add dilute hydrochloric acid from a burette, swirling the flask, until the indicator just changes colour (pink to colourless): the solution is exactly neutral. Record the volume of acid used.
3. Repeat with exactly the same volumes of alkali and acid, but **without the indicator**, so that the salt is not contaminated.
4. Heat the solution in an evaporating basin to evaporate part of the water until it is saturated (a drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals). Do not evaporate to dryness.
5. Leave the solution to cool and crystallise, then filter off the crystals.
6. Wash the crystals with a very small amount of cold distilled water and dry them between filter papers (or in a warm oven).

questions.enonce_markdown: Action of an acid on an insoluble base: using a suitable example, describe how a pure dry sample of the salt can be prepared. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Example: copper(II) sulphate from copper(II) oxide (an insoluble base) and dilute sulphuric acid.**

$\mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

1. Warm about $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of dilute sulphuric acid in a beaker (do not boil).
2. Add black copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring, until **no more dissolves** (some solid remains): the oxide is in excess, so all the acid has been used up. The solution turns blue.
3. **Filter** to remove the excess copper(II) oxide; the blue filtrate is copper(II) sulphate solution.
4. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until it is saturated (crystals form on a cold glass rod).
5. Allow it to cool slowly so that blue crystals of $\mathrm{CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O}$ form, and filter them off.
6. Wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter papers.

questions.enonce_markdown: Double decomposition: using a suitable example, describe how a pure dry sample of the salt can be prepared. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Double decomposition (precipitation) prepares an **insoluble** salt by mixing two soluble salts.

**Example: barium sulphate from barium chloride and sodium sulphate solutions.**

$\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_2SO_4(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$

1. Mix solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate in a beaker; a **white precipitate** of barium sulphate forms at once. Stir.
2. **Filter** the mixture; the barium sulphate stays on the filter paper and the soluble sodium chloride passes through in the filtrate.
3. **Wash** the residue on the filter paper with distilled water several times to remove the sodium chloride.
4. **Dry** the residue between filter papers or in a warm oven to obtain pure dry barium sulphate.
